overview: Finland was still a grand duchy within the Russian Empire when this map label begins in 1914. Parliament approved independence in December 1917, and a republic followed in 1919 after a bitter civil war. The continuing state’s history includes war, reconstruction, public services and innovations in design and science.

periods.title: The last years of the grand duchy
periods.summary: Finland had its own institutions within the Russian Empire before independence.

periods.title: Independence and the republic
periods.summary: Independence was followed by the 1918 civil war and a republican constitution in 1919.

periods.title: War and displacement
periods.summary: War brought territorial losses and the evacuation and resettlement of hundreds of thousands of people.

periods.title: Reconstruction and a continuing republic
periods.summary: Postwar Finland rebuilt and developed its public institutions and economy.

sections.title: Care, food and the design of daily life

items.text: Finland began providing maternity grants in 1938, initially for mothers with low incomes. In 1949, the benefit became available to all mothers. It could provide money or practical supplies, helping families prepare for a baby while connecting the scheme with public health services.

Early maternity packages included cloth and sewing patterns as well as ready-made clothing and other supplies. Some of the baby’s wardrobe therefore arrived as a project. The changing contents record how family work, shopping and expectations of public support developed over time.

A law passed in 1943 set a five-year timetable for free school meals. By 1948, elementary pupils were offered a daily meal such as soup or porridge, with milk and bread brought from home. School lunches developed gradually into the service familiar today.

The original school-meal arrangements asked pupils to help grow vegetables or gather berries for the kitchen, under their teacher’s guidance. Feeding a school involved gardens and forests as well as cooks. A child’s berries might become part of a later meal.

Alvar and Aino Aalto’s Paimio Sanatorium opened in 1933 for people with tuberculosis. The design included sun terraces, carefully chosen colors and dark ceilings in patients’ rooms. The architects considered what the building would feel like to someone spending long periods in bed.

Paimio’s surviving drawings include a washbasin designed to be quiet. Furniture and fittings were considered alongside the building itself, including the curved plywood Paimio chair. Even the sound of washing could become an architectural problem worth solving.

sections.title: Science, shared spaces and difficult memories

items.text: Artturi Virtanen developed a method in 1932 that used controlled acidity to preserve nutrients in cattle fodder. Keeping proteins and vitamins through the winter helped support milk production. His agricultural chemistry earned the 1945 Nobel Prize: scientific research could begin with the question of what cows would eat.

Helsinki’s Oodi library provides sewing worktables, electronics workstations and other equipment for making things. Its Urban Workspace connects learning with practical projects. A library visit can involve repairing clothes or working on a design as well as borrowing a book.

Oodi also offers recording, photography and video studios, with instruments and other equipment available through its library services. Residents can use the studios free of charge under the library’s booking rules. A public library can help people create stories and music, too.

In a Finnish sauna, water poured on hot stones produces löyly, the steam central to the experience. Families pass down customs, while public saunas create shared places to gather. Wood-fired, electric and other forms coexist within a tradition that includes both washing and quiet relaxation.

The 1918 civil war left political and personal divisions after the fighting ended. Many released prisoners lost voting and other civic rights, although most recovered them in the early 1920s. The history of the republic includes the long work of repairing relationships within society.

Finnish, section 1 of the 1919 Constitution Act: “Suomi on täysivaltainen tasavalta”. Translation: “Finland is a sovereign republic.” Finlex preserves this wording in its transcription of the original law of 17 July 1919, rather than silently substituting the later constitution.

ending.text: Finland continues as an independent republic. Its transition from Russian grand duchy to independent state took place in 1917, and the republican constitution followed in 1919. The map’s 1914 starting date belongs to the earlier imperial period.
